# The Principles of the Doctrine of Christ
Source: https://tpotdoc.com/
Updated: 2026-11-08

## Our Mission: What Does TPOTDOC Mean?
URL: https://tpotdoc.com/mission/

Our Mission
TPOTDOC… What?
TPOTDOC stands for The Principles Of The Doctrine Of Christ: the six foundation stones every new believer builds on, named in Hebrews 6:1–2.
Thank you for visiting this website! What a funny name, right? Well, I just wanted to let you know why the site is called TPOTDOC.
It’s based on a verse in the Bible, found in Hebrews 6:1–2. In that verse, the writer is talking about moving beyond these principles, which are also referred to as foundational. As I kept praying about building this reference site for new believers who are just coming to Christ, the Holy Spirit showed me these items in a new light, and that these are the best starting foundations for our faith in Christ.
— Yv'e Bridges

“Therefore leaving the principles of the doctrine of Christ, let us go on unto perfection; not laying again the foundation of repentance from dead works, and of faith toward God, of the doctrine of baptisms, and of laying on of hands, and of resurrection of the dead, and of eternal judgment.”
Hebrews 6:1–2 (KJV)

## What Is Repentance? Meaning of Metanoia (Greek G3341)
URL: https://tpotdoc.com/repentance/

Foundation Stone 1 · Word Study
What is repentance?
Repentance means changing your mind about sin and about God, and letting that change turn your whole life around.
The New Testament was first written in Greek. The word translated “repentance” is metanoia. It is built from two smaller words: meta, which carries the idea of “after” or “change,” and noeō, which means “to think” or “to understand.” Put together, it means to think differently afterward: to reconsider.
Three things happen when we repent
We see it differently. God opens our eyes, and we agree with Him that sin is wrong.
We feel it. The old word for this is compunction: a real, godly sorrow over sin. It is not shame that crushes us. It is sorrow that leads us to God.
We turn around. Repentance is a reversal of direction. We stop walking away from God and start walking with Him.
“For godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death.”
2 Corinthians 7:10
Fruit that fits repentance
John the Baptist preached to the Pharisees and Sadducees. These were religious people who trusted their birthright, their family line, and their traditions to save them. John told them that real repentance shows up in how we live.
“Bring forth therefore fruits meet for repentance.”
Matthew 3:8 · “meet” means fitting
That fruit is not something we produce by trying harder. It is what the Holy Spirit grows in us:
“But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, temperance: against such there is no law.”
Galatians 5:22–23
Recommended reading: Matthew 3:1–10, and Galatians 5:4–26, where the apostle Paul writes to people trying to be made right with God by keeping the law.
What are “dead works”?
Hebrews calls this “repentance from dead works.” Dead works are anything that cannot give life: the sins we used to live in, and also our own efforts to earn God’s approval. We turn away from both. Our new life comes from Jesus, not from trying harder.
“How much more shall the blood of Christ … purge your conscience from dead works to serve the living God?”
Hebrews 9:14
The good news
Repentance is not a punishment. It is a doorway. When we turn to God, He forgives and He refreshes.
“Repent ye therefore, and be converted, that your sins may be blotted out, when the times of refreshing shall come from the presence of the Lord.”
Acts 3:19
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
1 John 1:9
Have a question about repentance? Send it in and we will answer from the Word.
The Greek word
μετάνοια
metanoia · say it met-AN-oy-ah
Strong’s number
G3341 (noun, “repentance”)
Comes from
G3340 μετανοέω, metanoeō, “to repent” (met-an-o-EH-o)
Built from
G3326 meta · after, change + G3539 noeō · to think
Plain meaning
To think differently afterward; to reconsider, feel real sorrow for sin, and reverse direction.
From Yv'e’s study journal, Wednesday, September 23, 2026, 5:33 a.m.

## What Is Faith Toward God? Meaning of Pistis (Greek G4102)
URL: https://tpotdoc.com/faith/

Foundation Stone 2 · Word Study
What is faith toward God?
Faith means being persuaded that God is true, and leaning your whole weight on Jesus to save you.
The Greek word for faith is pistis. It comes from a verb that means “to persuade.” So faith begins when God convinces your heart that He is telling the truth.
Four sides of faith
Conviction. You are persuaded that God and His Word are true.
Reliance. You trust Christ, and Christ alone, for your salvation.
Constancy. You keep holding on, day after day.
The faith. The word can also mean the gospel itself: the truth we believe.
What did Jesus say about faith?
A Roman officer asked Jesus to heal his servant, and said Jesus only needed to speak the word. Jesus was amazed.
“When Jesus heard it, he marvelled, and said to them that followed, Verily I say unto you, I have not found so great faith, no, not in Israel.”
Matthew 8:10 · read Matthew 8:1–13
A woman who had been sick for twelve years believed that if she could only touch His garment, she would be healed.
“But Jesus turned him about, and when he saw her, he said, Daughter, be of good comfort; thy faith hath made thee whole. And the woman was made whole from that hour.”
Matthew 9:22 · read Matthew 9:20–22
God has given every believer “the measure of faith” (Romans 12:3).
The Greek word
πίστις
pistis · say it PIS-tis
Strong’s number
G4102 (noun, “faith”)
Comes from
G3982, “to persuade”
Plain meaning
Persuasion; a firm conviction that God is true; especially reliance on Christ for salvation.
Also translated
assurance, belief, believe, faith, fidelity
From Yv'e’s study journal, Wednesday, October 14, 2026, 5:52 a.m.

## Hebrew Roots of Baptism: Mikveh and Tevilah
URL: https://tpotdoc.com/baptisms/

Foundation Stone 3 · Hebrew Roots
What did baptism mean to the Jewish people in Jesus’ day?
Baptism was not a Christian invention. In the time of Jesus and John the Baptist, full-body immersion in water was already a deep part of Jewish life, a way of being made clean and starting over before God.
In Hebrew this immersion is called tevilah. It took place in a pool built for the purpose, called a mikveh, or in natural “living waters” like rivers and lakes.
Even the word in Hebrews 6:2 points back to this. “The doctrine of baptisms” uses the Greek word baptismos (G909), a washing. The same word is used for the “divers washings” of the Old Testament law.
“Which stood only in meats and drinks, and divers washings, and carnal ordinances, imposed on them until the time of reformation.”
Hebrews 9:10
How did the Jewish people understand immersion?
Being made clean. The Torah, in books like Leviticus, taught that water moved a person from being ritually unclean (tamei) to clean (tahor). Priests, pilgrims and everyday Jews immersed before entering the Temple, handling holy offerings, or keeping the feasts.
A new birth for converts. When a Gentile became a Jew, he was circumcised, offered a sacrifice, and was fully immersed. The rabbis spoke of the convert coming up out of the water like a newborn coming from the womb.
Turning back to God. Immersion was more than getting clean on the outside. It was a way of setting yourself apart, turning from the old ways, and drawing close to God.
Getting ready for God’s kingdom. Some groups, like the Essenes at Qumran, washed often as a sign of repentance. It showed they were separating from corruption and getting ready for the coming of God’s kingdom.
“… and he shall wash his clothes, and bathe his flesh in running water, and shall be clean.”
Leviticus 15:13
How does John the Baptist’s baptism fit in?
A call for the whole nation to repent. John drew on what his people already knew about being made clean and starting over. But his baptism was different. Temple washings were repeated again and again, and convert immersion was for Gentiles. John called all of Israel to repent and get right with God, because the Messiah and His kingdom were about to arrive.
“John did baptize in the wilderness, and preach the baptism of repentance for the remission of sins.”
Mark 1:4
Something they already understood. Because the people knew what immersion meant, nobody needed a brand-new explanation when John began baptizing in the Jordan River. They came out to him by the crowds.
“Then went out to him Jerusalem, and all Judaea, and all the region round about Jordan, and were baptized of him in Jordan, confessing their sins.”
Matthew 3:5–6
John also told them that Someone greater was coming, with a greater baptism:
“I indeed baptize you with water unto repentance: but he that cometh after me is mightier than I, whose shoes I am not worthy to bear: he shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost, and with fire.”
Matthew 3:11 · also Luke 3:16
John’s baptism in water prepared the people. Jesus would baptize with the Holy Ghost, and that promise came true on the day of Pentecost:
“And there appeared unto them cloven tongues like as of fire, and it sat upon each of them. And they were all filled with the Holy Ghost …”
Acts 2:3–4
Recommended reading: Matthew 3, Mark 1:1–11, Luke 3:1–22, and John 3:22–23.
What does “baptized for the dead” mean?
In 1 Corinthians 15, Paul writes the Bible’s great chapter on the resurrection. In the middle of it he mentions people who were “baptized for the dead”:
“Else what shall they do which are baptized for the dead, if the dead rise not at all? why are they then baptized for the dead?”
1 Corinthians 15:29
Paul was not teaching people to be baptized for someone who has died. Some in Corinth were doing this, and Paul used their own practice to make his point: why would anyone do this unless they believed the dead will rise again? Notice that Paul says “they,” not “we.” He is not making it a doctrine. He is showing how much the resurrection of the dead matters. If the dead do not rise, the practice means nothing, and so does our faith (1 Corinthians 15:17).
Salvation is for the living, by faith in Jesus. Each of us must believe for ourselves: “now is the accepted time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Corinthians 6:2). Read more in Foundation Stone 5: Resurrection.
Draft for Yv'e to review: adapted from the research on the Hebrew origins of baptism that she shared, November 2026. The Hebrews 9:10 link and the word card were added by Claude. The Pentecost paragraph and the wording of “baptized for the dead” were written by Claude from Yv'e’s position (Paul says “they,” not “we,” and uses their practice to show the importance of the resurrection), November 2026.
Have a question about baptism? Send it in and we will answer from the Word.
The Hebrew word
מִקְוֶה
miqveh · say it mik-VEH
Strong’s number
H4723 (noun)
Comes from
H6960 qavah, “to bind together, to collect; to wait for, to expect”
Plain meaning
A gathering of water, a pool; also something waited for, a hope.
In Scripture
“the gathering together of the waters” (Genesis 1:10); “O LORD, the hope of Israel” (Jeremiah 17:13)

## What Is the Laying On of Hands? (Hebrews 6:2)
URL: https://tpotdoc.com/laying-on-of-hands/

Foundation Stone 4 · Word Study
What is the laying on of hands?
The laying on of hands is placing your hands on a person while you pray, to bless them, to set them apart for God’s work, or to ask God to heal them or fill them with His Spirit.
“Of the doctrine of baptisms, and of laying on of hands, and of resurrection of the dead, and of eternal judgment.”
Hebrews 6:2
Where does the Bible first show it?
The first time is in Genesis 48. Jacob, also called Israel, was old and near death. Joseph brought his two sons to be blessed. Jacob crossed his arms on purpose and put his right hand, the hand of the greater blessing, on the younger son, Ephraim.
“And Israel stretched out his right hand, and laid it upon Ephraim’s head, who was the younger, and his left hand upon Manasseh’s head, guiding his hands wittingly; for Manasseh was the firstborn.”
Genesis 48:14
Three ways it was used in the Old Testament
In Hebrew this practice is called semikhah, from samak (H5564), “to lean upon.” The one laying on hands leaned his weight on the other.
To pass on a blessing. Jacob blessed his grandsons and spoke over their future (Genesis 48).
To place sin on a sacrifice. The worshipper laid his hand on the head of the animal offered for him. His sin was counted on the substitute, which died in his place (Leviticus 1:4; 16:21).
To give authority for God’s work. God told Moses to lay his hands on Joshua, to make him the next leader of Israel (Numbers 27:18–23).
“And he shall put his hand upon the head of the burnt offering; and it shall be accepted for him to make atonement for him.”
Leviticus 1:4
The sacrifices pointed to Jesus. On the cross, God laid our sin on Him, the perfect Lamb:
“All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned every one to his own way; and the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all.”
Isaiah 53:6
“And Joshua the son of Nun was full of the spirit of wisdom; for Moses had laid his hands upon him: and the children of Israel hearkened unto him, and did as the LORD commanded Moses.”
Deuteronomy 34:9
How did Jesus and the apostles lay on hands?
To bless. “And he took them up in his arms, put his hands upon them, and blessed them” (Mark 10:16).
To heal. “He laid his hands on every one of them, and healed them” (Luke 4:40). Jesus said of those who believe, “they shall lay hands on the sick, and they shall recover” (Mark 16:18).
To receive the Holy Ghost. “Then laid they their hands on them, and they received the Holy Ghost” (Acts 8:17).
To send people out for ministry. “And when they had fasted and prayed, and laid their hands on them, they sent them away” (Acts 13:3).
Because it is so serious, Paul told Timothy not to rush it: “Lay hands suddenly on no man” (1 Timothy 5:22).
Recommended reading: Genesis 48, Numbers 27:15–23, Acts 6:1–7, and Acts 8:14–17.
Draft for Yv'e to review: written by Claude from the research on the laying on of hands that she shared, November 2026. The New Testament verses, Isaiah 53:6, 1 Timothy 5:22 and the word card were added by Claude.
Have a question about the laying on of hands? Send it in and we will answer from the Word.
The Greek word
ἐπίθεσις
epithesis · say it ep-ITH-eh-sis
Strong’s number
G1936 (noun, “laying on”)
Comes from
G2007 ἐπιτίθημι, epitithēmi, “to lay upon”
Plain meaning
A putting on, especially of hands, to bless or set someone apart.
Hebrew background
H5564 samak, “to lean upon, to lay”

## What Is the Resurrection of the Dead? Bible Verses
URL: https://tpotdoc.com/resurrection/

Foundation Stone 5 · Word Study
What is the resurrection of the dead?
The resurrection of the dead is God’s promise that the bodies of the dead will be raised to life again, just as Jesus rose bodily from the grave.
The resurrection is not a small detail. It is where God’s whole plan of salvation is headed.
Did believers in the Old Testament hope for it?
Yes. Long before Jesus came, God’s people believed He would raise the dead.
“For I know that my redeemer liveth, and that he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth: And though after my skin worms destroy this body, yet in my flesh shall I see God.”
Job 19:25–26
“And many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.”
Daniel 12:2 · see also Isaiah 26:19 and Hosea 13:14
Jesus rose first
The resurrection of Jesus is the center of the Christian faith. He rose with a real body. He showed His disciples His hands and feet, and He ate with them.
“Behold my hands and my feet, that it is I myself: handle me, and see; for a spirit hath not flesh and bones, as ye see me have.”
Luke 24:39
More than 500 people saw Him alive at one time (1 Corinthians 15:3–8). Because He rose, everyone who belongs to Him will rise too.
“But now is Christ risen from the dead, and become the firstfruits of them that slept.”
1 Corinthians 15:20
People God raised back to life
The Bible tells of people who were raised from the dead. Each one shows God’s power over death:
Elijah and the widow’s son (1 Kings 17:17–24)
Elisha and the Shunammite woman’s son (2 Kings 4:32–37)
A man who touched Elisha’s bones (2 Kings 13:21)
The widow’s son at Nain (Luke 7:11–15)
Jairus’ daughter (Luke 8:49–56)
Lazarus, four days in the tomb (John 11:38–44)
Saints who came out of their graves after Jesus rose (Matthew 27:52–53)
Tabitha, also called Dorcas (Acts 9:36–42)
Eutychus, who fell from a window (Acts 20:9–12)
These people later died again. Jesus is different: “Christ being raised from the dead dieth no more; death hath no more dominion over him” (Romans 6:9).
What did Jesus teach about the resurrection?
“Jesus said unto her, I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live.”
John 11:25
“And this is the will of him that sent me, that every one which seeth the Son, and believeth on him, may have everlasting life: and I will raise him up at the last day.”
John 6:40
Jesus also taught that everyone will be raised, both the saved and the lost:
“Marvel not at this: for the hour is coming, in the which all that are in the graves shall hear his voice, And shall come forth; they that have done good, unto the resurrection of life; and they that have done evil, unto the resurrection of damnation.”
John 5:28–29 · see also Acts 24:15
Why does the resurrection matter?
Paul says that without the resurrection, our faith would be empty:
“And if Christ be not raised, your faith is vain; ye are yet in your sins.”
1 Corinthians 15:17
But Christ is raised, and so we have hope when someone we love dies in the Lord. When Jesus comes back, they will rise first:
“For the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God: and the dead in Christ shall rise first: Then we which are alive and remain shall be caught up together with them in the clouds, to meet the Lord in the air: and so shall we ever be with the Lord.”
1 Thessalonians 4:16–17
“In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trump: for the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed.”
1 Corinthians 15:52
Paul even pointed to people who were “baptized for the dead” to show how much the resurrection matters. The Bible ends with the dead raised, some to reign with Christ (Revelation 20:4–6), and all to stand before God (Revelation 20:11–13).
Recommended reading: John 11:1–44, Luke 24, 1 Corinthians 15 (the resurrection chapter), and 1 Thessalonians 4:13–18.
Draft for Yv'e to review: written by Claude from the list of resurrection Scriptures that she shared, November 2026. Romans 6:9 and the word card were added by Claude.
Have a question about the resurrection? Send it in and we will answer from the Word.
The Greek word
ἀνάστασις
anastasis · say it an-AS-tah-sis
Strong’s number
G386 (noun, “resurrection”)
Comes from
G450 ἀνίστημι, anistēmi, “to stand up”
Built from
G303 ana · up, again + G2476 histēmi · to stand
Plain meaning
A standing up again; a rising from death to life.

## What Is Eternal Judgment? What Jesus Taught
URL: https://tpotdoc.com/eternal-judgment/

Foundation Stone 6 · Word Study
What is eternal judgment?
Eternal judgment is the final judgment of every person by Jesus Christ. His verdict lasts forever: everlasting life for those who belong to Him, and everlasting punishment for those who reject Him.
“And as it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment.”
Hebrews 9:27
Who is the Judge?
Jesus Himself. The Father has given Him all authority to judge.
“For the Father judgeth no man, but hath committed all judgment unto the Son: That all men should honour the Son, even as they honour the Father.”
John 5:22–23 · see also John 5:27
How did Jesus describe the final judgment?
Jesus used everyday pictures to show that at the end of the age, people will be divided into two groups:
Sheep and goats. When He comes in His glory, He will separate the nations “as a shepherd divideth his sheep from the goats” (Matthew 25:31–46).
Wheat and tares. Good grain and weeds grow together until the harvest, and then they are separated (Matthew 13:24–30, 36–43).
The net. A net gathers every kind of fish, and then the good are kept and the bad thrown away (Matthew 13:47–50).
“And these shall go away into everlasting punishment: but the righteous into life eternal.”
Matthew 25:46
What will be judged?
Our words. “Every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment” (Matthew 12:36).
How we treat others. “Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me” (Matthew 25:40).
Whether we really know Him. Calling Him “Lord, Lord” is not enough. To some He will say, “I never knew you: depart from me, ye that work iniquity” (Matthew 7:21–23).
“And I saw the dead, small and great, stand before God; and the books were opened: and another book was opened, which is the book of life: and the dead were judged out of those things which were written in the books, according to their works.”
Revelation 20:12
What did Jesus say about hell?
Jesus spoke about hell more than anyone else in the Bible. He used the word Gehenna, the name of a valley outside Jerusalem where fires burned. He called it a place “where their worm dieth not, and the fire is not quenched” (Mark 9:44), and a place of “weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matthew 8:12). He warned us because He does not want anyone to go there.
The good news: you do not have to fear judgment
Jesus came to save us from judgment, not to condemn us.
“For God sent not his Son into the world to condemn the world; but that the world through him might be saved. He that believeth on him is not condemned: but he that believeth not is condemned already, because he hath not believed in the name of the only begotten Son of God.”
John 3:17–18
“Verily, verily, I say unto you, He that heareth my word, and believeth on him that sent me, hath everlasting life, and shall not come into condemnation; but is passed from death unto life.”
John 5:24
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus …”
Romans 8:1
If you have turned to God in repentance and put your faith in Jesus, you have passed from death to life. That is where these six foundations began.
Recommended reading: Matthew 25:31–46, John 5:19–30, and Revelation 20:11–15.
Draft for Yv'e to review: written by Claude from the research on what Christ taught about eternal judgment that she shared, November 2026. Hebrews 9:27, Revelation 20:12, Romans 8:1 and the word card were added by Claude.
Have a question about eternal judgment? Send it in and we will answer from the Word.
The Greek words
κρίμα αἰώνιον
krima aiōnion · say it KREE-mah eye-OH-nee-on
Judgment
G2917 krima, from G2919 krinō, “to distinguish, to decide, to judge”
Eternal
G166 aiōnios, from G165 aiōn, “an age”; lasting forever
Plain meaning
A final verdict that will never change.

## Neither Barren nor Unfruitful: 2 Peter 1:8 Word Study
URL: https://tpotdoc.com/fruitful/

Word Study · Growing in Christ
Neither barren nor unfruitful
God did not save you to sit still. He planted a new life in you, and it is meant to grow and bear fruit.
Peter gives new believers a simple plan for growth. Start with faith, and keep adding to it:
Faith
Virtue
Knowledge
Temperance
Patience
Godliness
Brotherly kindness
Charity (love)
“For if these things be in you, and abound, they make you that ye shall neither be barren nor unfruitful in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ.”
2 Peter 1:8
Two Greek words in that verse show what God is keeping us from. Both begin with the little letter a-, which means “without,” the same way “a-” works in the English word atypical.
“Barren”
ἀργός
argos · say it ar-GOS
Strong’s number
G692
Built from
a- · without + ergon · work
Plain meaning
Without work: inactive, unemployed. By implication, lazy or useless. Translated barren, idle, slow.
“Unfruitful”
ἄκαρπος
akarpos · say it AK-ar-pos
Strong’s number
G175
Built from
a- · without + karpos · fruit
Plain meaning
Without fruit. Barren, whether a field that grows nothing or a life that shows nothing of God.
What this means for you
Remember the first foundation stone: we repent from dead works, things we did to earn God’s favor. Now Peter shows the other side. Once we belong to Jesus, our faith is not meant to sit without work or without fruit. As we add these qualities day by day, God makes our lives busy with His purposes and full of His fruit.
From Yv'e’s study journal, October 13, 2026.

## Questions New Believers Ask
URL: https://tpotdoc.com/questions/

Questions & Answers
Has someone asked this already?
Search the questions other new believers have asked. If you don’t find yours, send it in.
Search questions
How do I know I really repented?
If you are asking this question, God is already at work in your heart. Here is what the Word shows us:
Look at what happened inside. Did you see your sin differently, feel godly sorrow, and turn toward God? Those are the three things that happen when we repent.
Look for fruit over time. Real repentance shows in how we live, as the Holy Spirit grows His fruit in us. See fruit that fits repentance (Matthew 3:8; Galatians 5:22–23).
Rest on God’s promise, not your feelings. “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins” (1 John 1:9). God wrote His Word “that ye may know that ye have eternal life” (1 John 5:13).
I’m a new believer. Where should I start reading the Bible?
Start in the New Testament, with the Gospel of John or the Gospel of Mark. John was written “that ye might believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God; and that believing ye might have life through his name” (John 20:31).
Good books to start with
John: who Jesus is, why He came, and what it means to believe in Him.
Mark: a short, fast-moving account of Jesus’ life, miracles, ministry, death and resurrection.
Luke, then Acts: the life of Jesus, followed by the birth and spread of the early church.
James: a short, practical letter full of everyday wisdom for living as a Christian.
Where to go next
The letters, such as Ephesians, Philippians and Romans, to learn what we believe and how to live it out.
Psalms and Proverbs, a little each day, for prayer, comfort and wisdom.
Genesis, when you are ready for the Old Testament and the beginning of God’s story.
Tips for beginners
Read a little every day. Even one chapter is enough. Pray first, and focus on getting to know Jesus.
Don’t be troubled by hard parts. Ask the Holy Spirit to teach you (John 14:26), and send us your question.
Connect with a church. Study with others where you can ask questions and grow together. See churches we recommend.
Don’t have a Bible of your own? Ask for a free one and Yv'e will mail it to you (U.S. only, while supplies last). For another reading plan, see Billy Graham’s answer, “Where should I begin in my Bible reading?”

## Scripture Prayers for Everyday Needs
URL: https://tpotdoc.com/prayers/

Scripture Prayers
Prayers from God’s Word for everyday needs
A Scripture prayer is a prayer built from God’s own promises, so you can pray with confidence that you are asking according to His will.
“And this is the confidence that we have in him, that, if we ask any thing according to his will, he heareth us.”
1 John 5:14
Pray these out loud. Put your own name in them. A new prayer is added often. If you need prayer for something not listed here, send a prayer request and Yv'e will pray for you personally.
Prayer 1
A prayer before a test
“If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God, that giveth to all men liberally, and upbraideth not; and it shall be given him.”
James 1:5
“For God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind.”
2 Timothy 1:7
“Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God. And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus.”
Philippians 4:6–7
Pray
Father God, thank You that You give wisdom freely to everyone who asks, so I ask You for wisdom today. You have not given me a spirit of fear, but of power, of love, and of a sound mind. I receive Your peace over my heart and my mind. Help me remember what I have studied, think clearly, and do my very best for Your glory. Whatever the result, I trust You. In Jesus’ name, amen.
Draft for Yv'e to review: this prayer was written for her, not taken from her notes.
Prayer 2
When I am tested or tempted
In the Bible, one Greek word covers both being tested and being tempted. Jesus faced it too, so He understands exactly what you are going through.
“Tempted” in Hebrews 4:15
πειράζω
peirazō · say it pi-RAD-zo
Strong’s number
G3985, from G3984
Plain meaning
To test or try something to see what it is made of: to examine, prove, scrutinize, or entice. Translated assay, examine, go about, prove, tempt, try.
“For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin. Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need.”
Hebrews 4:15–16
“There hath no temptation taken you but such as is common to man: but God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape, that ye may be able to bear it.”
1 Corinthians 10:13
“Blessed is the man that endureth temptation: for when he is tried, he shall receive the crown of life, which the Lord hath promised to them that love him.”
James 1:12
Pray
Lord Jesus, thank You that You were tested in every way I am, yet without sin, so You understand what I am facing right now. I come boldly to Your throne of grace for mercy and for help. Father, You are faithful. You will not let me be tested beyond what I can bear, and You have already made a way of escape. Show me that way, and give me the strength to take it. Help me endure and come through this stronger in You. In Jesus’ name, amen.
The word study is from Yv'e’s journal, October 28, 2026. The prayer is a draft for her to review.

## About Dianna "Yv'e" Bridges
URL: https://tpotdoc.com/about/

About
Meet Yv'e Bridges
Dianna “Yv'e” Bridges has taught the Word of God to children, youth and adults for decades.
Yv'e gave her life to Jesus on March 25, 1983, at her daddy’s house in the Spring Branch area of Houston, Texas. Since then she has served in children’s ministries and choirs for decades, in Houston, in the Daytona Beach, Florida area, and in the Dallas–Fort Worth Metroplex.
From the late 1990s into the 2000s, she served alongside Pam and Robert White at Kids for Christ Elementary, the children’s ministry of Calvary Cathedral. She also served three years as a lay counselor at a crisis pregnancy center, and has spoken to youth groups, to a crowd of about 2,000 at a pro-life rally in Peabody Auditorium in Daytona Beach in 1990, and in women’s and singles ministries.
She is the author of Praying A to Z and the Kids for Christ “Bring Them Home!” Witnessing Workbook. She started this site to give new believers a strong foundation, built on the six principles of Hebrews 6:1–2.
Written from Yv'e’s own notes. Yv'e, please check the details and wording.

## Privacy
URL: https://tpotdoc.com/privacy/

Privacy
Your privacy on this site
We collect only what you choose to send us, we never sell it, and we use it for one thing: to answer you and pray for you.
What we collect
The only information this site gathers is what you type into the Ask & Pray form: your first name, your email address if you give it, the topic, and your message. If you ask for a free Bible, we also collect your name and mailing address, and we use them only to mail you the Bible. Nothing is collected when you simply read the lessons.
How it is delivered
Form messages are delivered to Yv'e’s inbox by FormSubmit (formsubmit.co), a form-delivery service. The message passes through their servers on the way. Yv'e, and anyone she personally asks to help answer prayer requests, reads it. We do not post your request publicly, and we do not share your email or mailing address with anyone else.
Cookies and tracking
This site sets no cookies and shows no advertising. It does not use Google Fonts or other third-party services that track you. To learn which lessons are most helpful, we count page views with Cloudflare Web Analytics, which uses no cookies and does not identify you or follow you to other sites.
Links to other sites
We link to churches, ministries and prayer lines we recommend. Each of those sites has its own privacy practices, which we do not control.
Children
This site is written for people of all ages who are new to Christ. We do not knowingly collect information from children under 13. If a child has sent us a message, a parent or guardian may ask us to delete it.
Your choices
You may ask us at any time to delete a message you sent, any reply, and any mailing address you gave us. Just send a note through the Ask & Pray form.
Last updated October 29, 2026.
